crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
children.blurb: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines cover the practices and tools that let a quantitative analysis be re-run and produce the same result.

children.name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
children.blurb: Asking data questions in plain language means a person types a question such as "which regions grew fastest last quarter" and a system translates it into a query against a database, spreadsheet, or data warehouse.

children.name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
children.blurb: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the systems and practices used to run heavy analytical and machine learning workloads over datasets that an organization holds under its own rules, such as university research archives, hospital records, government registers, and corporate transaction logs.

children.name: Writing Statistical Code with AI
children.blurb: Writing statistical code with AI covers using AI assistants to draft, refactor, explain, and test code for statistical analysis, data cleaning, modeling, and visualization.

children.name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
children.blurb: Testing a study design before data collection means checking whether a planned quantitative study can answer its question with the data it expects to gather.

sections.body: Quantitative analysis and reproducible work is the part of AI research that turns a question into numbers that can be checked. In practice, AI systems now help write statistical code, suggest appropriate tests, and assemble notebooks that record each step. They can translate a plain language question into a database query or an analysis plan, then run that plan on large institutional datasets. They also help capture software versions, random seeds, and parameter choices so that a result can be rerun later. This work is less about replacing the analyst and more about making the path from raw data to reported claim visible. The aim is a result that another person can inspect, rerun, and challenge with the same data and code.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are settled, including version control, notebook execution, and dependency capture, and AI can generate working code for common statistical tasks. The hard parts remain. Code produced by AI can be syntactically correct and statistically wrong, and it often hides assumptions that a human must check. Plain language questions are ambiguous, so translation into a query can silently change the meaning of the analysis. Large scale compute on institutional data raises access, privacy, and cost problems that no notebook alone can solve, and testing a study design before data collection still depends on assumptions that may not hold. The site library holds 135 research papers, and even at that scale, checking every analysis by hand is not feasible, which is why automated reproducibility checks matter.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to make an analysis repeatable would start with Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines, which covers the mechanics of capturing code, data, and environment. Asking Data Questions in Plain Language addresses the front end, where a researcher states a question and an AI system translates it into a query or an analysis plan. Writing Statistical Code with AI goes deeper into code generation, testing, and the review needed before trusting output. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data covers the infrastructure side, including access controls, job scheduling, and cost. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection shows how simulation and pilot analysis can reveal problems before data is gathered. Together these pages move from question to design to code to execution to reproducibility.
